item.research_question: How to achieve a simultaneous balance of high fracture strength and high ductility in high-entropy alloys while overcoming inferior castability and compositional segregation?
item.processing_route: Vacuum induction melting of commercially pure elements (Al, Co, Ni: 99.9 wt.%; Cr, Fe: 99.5 ~ 99.6 wt.%) in a BN crucible; heating to 600°C for 1 hour; pouring at 1500°C into a MgO crucible (220 mm length, 62 mm upper ID, 50 mm bottom ID) under argon atmosphere (0.06 MPa); bulk ingot weight ~2.5 kg.
item.test_conditions: Room temperature tensile tests at strain rate 1 × 10−3 s−1; elevated temperature tests at 600°C and 700°C at strain rate 1 × 10−3 s−1; cold rolling with 8% thickness reduction followed by tensile testing at 2 × 10−3 s−1.
key_findings: The as-cast alloy exhibited a fine lamellar fcc/B2 microstructure with an inter-lamellar spacing of about 2 μm.
Room temperature tensile test showed a fracture stress of 944 MPa and an elongation of 25.6%.
The proof stress was 75 MPa, while the fracture stress reached close to 1.2 GPa (true stress condition).
At 600°C, the alloy maintained a fracture stress of 806 MPa and elongation of 33.7%.
At 700°C, the alloy maintained a fracture stress of 538 MPa and elongation of 22.9%.
Cold rolling with 8% reduction increased the true fracture stress to 1265 MPa while maintaining 9.9% elongation.
The density of the EHEA was measured to be 7.38 g/cm3.
The ratio of fracture strength to proof stress (σUTS/σ0.2) was close to 16.
item.mechanism: The authors attribute the unprecedented strain hardening and balanced properties to the fine regular lamellar structure that easily stores dislocations and the alternating soft fcc phases and hard B2-structured NiAl-rich phases. When dislocations pass through soft fcc phases, the hard B2 phases, including nanoscale precipitates, pin the movement of dislocations resulting in significant work hardening.
item.limitations: The text notes that the mechanism for the low elastic limit (proof stress) is still unclear at this stage.
item.future_work: Further exploration of new EHEAs will be based on physical metallurgy principles using atomic radius, mixing enthalpy, and valence electron concentration; thermodynamics calculations based on the CALPHAD method can provide guidance once reliable databases are established; the potential for producing ultrahigh strength components after large plastic deformation awaits further investigations.
quotes: To tackle these problems, here we proposed a novel strategy to design HEAs using the eutectic alloy concept, i.e. to achieve a microstructure composed of alternating soft fcc and hard bcc phases.
The room temperature tensile test showed a fracture stress of 944 MPa and an elongation of 25.6%, from the engineering stress-strain curve given in Fig. 4a.
Such a high σUTS/σ0.2 is also far beyond those of conventional alloys, which are in the range of 1 ~ 3.
